title: MotoGP signs two-year ESPN media rights deal for U.S., Latin America
article_text:
MotoGP signs two-year ESPN media rights deal for U.S., Latin America

MotoGP named ESPN its exclusive U.S. rights holder on linear networks for 2027 and 2028. A two-year deal gives sponsors and production teams a fixed U.S. partner to plan around, though only for two seasons.

This story was produced through MarketScale. See how Sports & Entertainment teams put it to work with Events & Onsite Capture.

MotoGP has announced a two-year media rights deal that puts the series on ESPN in the United States and Latin America across the 2027 and 2028 seasons. In the title race, ESPN's Austin Lindberg reports that Marc Márquez holds a 60-point lead over Jorge Martín, the 2024 world champion. Márquez got there by overcoming a record 102-point deficit, and he is now in position to clinch a record-equaling eighth MotoGP world championship. Two rounds remain, in Portugal and Valencia, and 74 points are still available.

The new home is ESPN. Under a two-year agreement covering the 2027 and 2028 seasons, ESPN becomes MotoGP's exclusive U.S. media rights holder across its linear networks, and it keeps its long-running coverage in key Latin American markets, including streaming on Disney+ Plan Premium, Sports Video Group reported. ESPN succeeds Fox Sports as the U.S. rights holder, SportBusiness's Jonathan Rest wrote, and MotoGP said its current U.S. arrangement ends with the 2026 season.

Timing matters as much as the network. The deal was announced on Nov. 12, 2026, ahead of the 2027 season. A two-year U.S. deal gives MotoGP's broadcast and commercial partners a known U.S. home for 2027 and 2028. For a sponsor sizing U.S. exposure or a production lead booking crews and studio time, that is the difference between a plan and a guess.

The Race laid out how often MotoGP's American carrier has changed. The sequence, by its account:

- ESPN, 2027 and 2028, announced Nov. 12, 2026

The Race also noted that under recent arrangements, coverage moved around between channels, and that during the NBC years many races did not air live. In its view the TNT deal did not prove substantially different. The Fox years followed the same pattern: this year's American Grand Prix at Austin aired live on Fox Business.

Against that record, the announcement date is the real change. The last two U.S. deals were confirmed with hours to spare. This one arrives while the 2026 season still has two rounds to run. The Race said it would finally give the series a more permanent U.S. TV home.

Early notice and channel stability are two separate things, and the announcement settles only the first. The release commits ESPN to airing Grand Prix events on "ESPN networks and platforms" either live or on same-day delay. The race-by-race channel assignments for 2027 have not been published yet.

Same-day delay is the release's fallback to live. A Grand Prix that is not shown as it happens still airs on ESPN networks and platforms on race day. The Race read the commitment as live or same-day coverage of every round, so for U.S. viewers the share of rounds aired live becomes the measure that matters, given how many NBC-era races missed live air.

ESPN did not win the U.S. rights as a stranger. It has carried MotoGP in Latin America for more than two decades, and both parties framed the U.S. expansion as growth from that base.

Freddy Rolón, head of ESPN's Global Sports & Talent Office, described the deal in the joint announcement as an example of a relationship that starts in one region of ESPN's international business and grows across its global portfolio. Carlos Ezpeleta, MotoGP's deputy CEO, called it a milestone in the championship's growth strategy across the Americas and pointed to ESPN's reach with audiences in both the U.S. and Latin America.

The pattern suggests a lesson for rights sellers and buyers alike. A regional partner with a long track record carries a credential into adjacent territories: the production relationship, the commercial terms and the working knowledge of the property already exist. For media companies holding regional rights to a property with an unsettled U.S. home, the ESPN route indicates that performance in one region can earn a seat at the bigger table.

In Latin America, ESPN networks will carry the races and Disney+ Plan Premium will stream them. In Argentina and Brazil, the agreement allows rights to select events to be sublicensed to local free-to-air broadcasters. MotoGP's release describes those two countries as among its most passionate markets.

That carve-out lets an exclusive pay and streaming deal sit alongside open-air reach for chosen races, so the series can chase casual viewers in its strongest markets without giving up the exclusive partner. The commercial terms of the sublicensing were not part of the announcement. For free-to-air broadcasters in Argentina and Brazil, though, the agreement confirms that a path to select MotoGP events exists for 2027 and 2028.

The Race described Liberty Media as the series' new owner, and both trade titles read the deal through that lens. SportBusiness framed it as ESPN getting back into business with Liberty in the U.S. The Race saw a growth platform for an owner trying to repeat its Formula 1 success in the American market.

MotoGP's own release lays out the growth case: it cites record-breaking attendance, expanding global audiences and increasing interest across the Americas. Ezpeleta called the deal "an exciting opportunity to introduce MotoGP to new audiences while continuing to serve our passionate existing fanbase." That two-track aim maps onto the deal's shape: new U.S. reach on ESPN's linear networks, and continuity for an audience ESPN has served in Latin America since 2002.

title: JTBC, ‘For Sale,’ Gives Up Olympic Broadcast Rights... Shedding the ‘Winner’s Curse’
article_text:
[Sportschosun reporter Baek Ji-eun] JTBC has given up Olympic broadcasting.

On the 16th, JTBC said, “The broadcast rights agreement between our company and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has been terminated because the rehabilitation proceedings have made it difficult to continue the Olympic broadcasting business.”

In 2019, JTBC bought exclusive rights from the IOC to broadcast the Summer and Winter Olympics from 2026 to 2032 for approximately 500 billion to 600 billion won. It then secured broadcast rights for the 2026–2030 FIFA World Cup as well. JTBC had tried to resell the rights to the three terrestrial broadcasters—Korean Broadcasting System (KBS), Seoul Broadcasting System (SBS) and Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation (MBC)—but they refused to buy them, citing the high price, so JTBC decided to switch to exclusive coverage.

But financial difficulties proved a stumbling block. External headwinds—including the collapse of the broadcast advertising market and soaring production costs for dramas and variety shows—were compounded by cash shortages and a liquidity crisis at JoongAng Group. In the end, JTBC failed to repay about 20.6 billion won in securitized borrowings last June and declared default. In August, JTBC received a court order to begin rehabilitation proceedings from the Seoul Bankruptcy Court, and in October, with court approval, it began pursuing an M&A before the rehabilitation plan is approved.

On the 9th, Ernst & Young Han Young, the lead manager for JTBC’s sale, issued a sale notice, saying that the sale would proceed through open competitive bidding, with external capital to be raised through measures including a paid-in capital increase via third-party allotment and the issuance of corporate bonds.

JTBC’s decision to give up the Olympic broadcast rights is a painful measure to eliminate uncertainty over its future liabilities.

Under court-supervised rehabilitation, unperformed contracts can be legally terminated. Because JTBC terminated the contract, it must absorb the loss of the contract payment already made to the IOC and pay a penalty. But it chose a big bath, recording the costs as non-operating losses unrelated to operating profit. If it clears out all its losses this year, the lower cost burden next year could make its results appear to improve sharply. It has also eliminated uncertainty around the sale of the company stemming from the possibility that it might need several hundred billion won more for Olympic broadcast rights in the future. JTBC had already achieved a turnaround, recording operating profit of 1.7 billion won in August, and expects operating profit of around 3 billion won in September. This will allow it to appeal to prospective buyers as a sound broadcaster whose core businesses—dramas, variety shows and news—are profitable.

JTBC said, “The costs resulting from the termination of the contract will be determined following the third-quarter accounting treatment and in accordance with the rehabilitation plan to be approved later. By recording in our accounts the losses anticipated under the rehabilitation proceedings, we will resolve uncertainty over funding and continue the upward trend in operating profit based on our core business.” It added, “We plan to communicate closely with the IOC through various channels and address the issues resulting from the termination of the broadcast rights agreement. Coverage of future Olympics, including the 2028 LA Olympics, will be handled by a new rights-holding broadcaster or consortium.”

With JTBC’s exclusive broadcast rights deal scrapped, the IOC will sign new agreements with other platforms for broadcast rights in South Korea, which will then air the events.

Reporter Baek Ji-eun silk781220@sportschosun.com

title: Dana White's UFC fighter loan system faces scrutiny after RAF Abu Dhabi brawl arrests
article_text:
Dana White's UFC fighter loan system faces scrutiny following a series of violent incidents at Real American Freestyle wrestling events.

Merab Dvalishvili was involved in a fight by a group led by Usman Nurmagomedov in Abu Dhabi, resulting in 10 arrests and multiple convictions.

Usman Nurmagomedov's prospective UFC signing and his brother Umar's career prospects have been severely damaged by their six-month prison sentences.

The UFC has a history of tolerating pre-fight confrontations, with incidents involving Conor McGregor and others having become defining moments in the sport.

"It's crazy. I mean, they must like it for this to happen all the time," UFC president Dana White said of the recurring incidents.

Dana White has built a global sporting empire on the backs of fighters who are as adept at selling a fight outside the octagon as they are at winning one inside it.

But the UFC president may be discovering that when his stars step outside the organisation, the theatre of pre-fight promotion can spill over into something altogether more serious.

White has been happy to see some of his biggest names compete on Real American Freestyle (RAF) wrestling cards. But a series of ugly confrontations, culminating in last week's extraordinary scenes in Abu Dhabi, could force him to reconsider.

Initially, letting his MMA fighters compete on RAF wrestling cards made sense. There's no striking involved, so the risk of serious injuries and concussions is greatly reduced. It keeps athletes active in between fights and exposes them to a new audience.

To recap, Merab Dvalishvili, the former UFC bantamweight champion, was ambushed by a group led by fellow MMA fighter Usman Nurmagomedov in the lobby of the Yas Hilton hotel ahead of his appearance at RAF Abu Dhabi.

Police made 10 arrests. The Abu Dhabi Criminal Court subsequently convicted eight of those involved, with Dvalishvili and his accomplice, Saba Lazishvili, fined Dh50,000 each and released.

Footage of the attack went viral. Two of those convicted were jailed after publishing footage of the brawl.

It was bad for everyone involved, not least the Nurmagomedovs. Usman was in talks to sign with the UFC after becoming a free agent following the expiration of his PFL contract. Umar was already on the UFC roster. It is hard to see how either has a future in the organisation.

It followed another high-profile brawl involving two of White's star UFC names at the pre-fight press conference ahead of RAF 14 last month.

On that occasion, Arman Tsarukyan tried to get at Dillon Danis, a rent-a-gob jiu-jitsu practitioner who likes to antagonise his opponents with racial slurs and provocative statements.

Danis wore a T-shirt that depicted Khamzat Chimaev, another stud in the UFC stable who was sat in the front row, in a less than favourable light. A melee ensued before security got control of the situation.

That was spillover from Danis' loss to Chimaev at RAF 10. The UAE combat star pinned Danis in 44 seconds and kicked him up the backside as he lay on the mat after the referee's whistle, resulting in members of both teams storming the stage.

On Sunday, White was asked if the UFC was reconsidering loaning their fighters out to the RAF following a spate of incidents.

"It's crazy. I mean, they must like it for this to happen all the time," White said, shaking his head.

His frustration is understandable. A deal for Usman, the undefeated PFL lightweight champion and a genuine star, looks dead in the water. His brother Umar, a former world title contender at bantamweight, is unlikely to fight again until at least the back end of 2027, if he is retained at all.

Dvalishvili, the former UFC bantamweight champion, was lucky to suffer only cuts and bruises to his face following the attack. That he competed at RAF Abu Dhabi this past Saturday – and then called for Usman and his associates to be immediately released – is a testament to his character.

It's important to acknowledge that the UFC does RAF a favour in loaning out its fighters to compete against genuine world-class wrestlers and Olympians. It elevates RAF, something CEO and co-founder Chad Bronstein acknowledges.

But from White's perspective, the CEO of a multibillion-dollar company doesn't want his fighters involved in violent altercations unless they are in the confines of a UFC octagon.

It also seems a bit rich that a man happy to let flames be fanned to sell a fight in his own organisation objects to it being done in others.

Fighters taking it to each other ahead of fights or at press conferences is nothing new, and certainly not in the UFC.

Conor McGregor specialised in it. Before his first fight with Nate Diaz in 2016, he and his camp exchanged insults and threw water bottles and cans at each other as the event descended into mayhem.

The Irishman and his entourage attacked a bus carrying Khabib Nurmagomedov – the trainer and cousin of Usman and Umar – and other fighters at Barclays Centre in Brooklyn ahead of UFC 299.

The incident left several fighters injured and became one of the defining moments in UFC history. The rivalry culminated in a post-fight brawl after Khabib submitted McGregor at UFC 229.

During a promotional press conference ahead of UFC 178, light-heavyweight rivals Jon Jones and Daniel Cormier went head-to-head before Jones shoved Cormier. Both fighters started swinging, knocking over the promotional backdrop and sending security scrambling.

title: Cricket Victoria Foundation Partners with Straight Bat Private Equity
article_text:
The Cricket Victoria Foundation has announced a new philanthropic and corporate partnership with Australian investment firm Straight Bat Private Equity to expand grassroots cricket access and community leadership initiatives across Victoria.

The agreement integrates Straight Bat into the Foundation’s flagship donor network as a Champion member of the First XI programme, while directing funding toward core community impact initiatives across the state.

Named after cricket’s hallmark principles of fair play and reliability, Straight Bat Private Equity specialises in long-term capital partnerships with established, medium-sized Australian businesses.

Under the partnership framework, Straight Bat will support the Foundation’s three primary strategic pillars, Access to the Game, Building the Future, and Strengthening Community Wellbeing, building on a previous season that engaged more than 1,000 Victorians through grassroots participation, female club leadership programmes, and the Scott Boland Indigenous Scholarship.

Cricket Victoria head of foundation, Ben Brennan, highlighted the shared values uniting corporate teamwork with community sports development.

“We’re delighted to welcome Straight Bat Private Equity as a partner of the Cricket Victoria Foundation.”

“Their focus on relationships, teamwork and supporting one another reflects our belief in cricket’s ability to bring people together and create opportunities.

“We look forward to working together and welcoming Straight Bat’s business community and their families to Junction Oval this month,” Brennan said.

Straight Bat Private Equity managing partner, Steve Gledden, emphasised the firm’s long-standing cultural connection to cricket and its commitment to backing community pathways.

“When we started Straight Bat, we signed cricket bats alongside the founders of the first businesses we backed.”

“That’s become one of our traditions. Putting our names alongside one another is our way of saying, ‘You can count on us.

“We know what a difference it makes to have someone back you, whether you’re building a business or finding your feet at a local club.

“Last season, the Foundation reached more than 1,000 Victorians.

“It helps people find a team to play for, gives women and girls the chance to lead in their clubs and, through the Scott Boland Indigenous Scholarship, supports First Nations students to study business and leadership.

“We’re proud to help the Foundation give more Victorians that kind of backing,” Gledden said.

title: Sportico: NBA 2025-26 revenue $14.5B; teams got $13.7B
article_text:
Sportico: NBA 2025-26 revenue $14.5B; teams got $13.7B

Sportico estimates the NBA made about $14.5 billion in 2025-26, with the 30 clubs taking in $13.7 billion, or $456 million apiece. Team revenue ranged from $895 million for Golden State to $339 million for Memphis, both after revenue sharing. Media-rights payouts rise about 7% a year on average. Local business—tickets, sponsorships and arena events—helps explain much of the gap between clubs.

This story was produced through MarketScale. See how Sports & Entertainment teams put it to work with Events & Onsite Capture.

Sportico's Kurt Badenhausen published a full breakdown of NBA finances on October 20. He puts the NBA's 2025-26 revenue at roughly $14.5 billion. The 30 clubs took in $13.7 billion of that, or $456 million apiece.

The team total includes concerts and other non-NBA events at arenas the clubs own or run. The league keeps part of the $14.5 billion at its own level to cover investments and expenses. For anyone who sells to, sponsors or operates alongside an NBA club, the more useful question is where the new money came from. Most of it came from a single contract.

The last figure is the one finance teams will care about most. Payouts rise about 7% a year on average, so the largest single line in a club's budget can be modeled a decade out. Gate receipts can't. Ticket money depends on who wins. The TV escalator doesn't.

The baseline helps here. In 2022, Front Office Sports reported that media rights made up roughly $2.6 billion of the league's annual revenue. The new deals are worth $6.9 billion a year, more than two and a half times that figure.

Sportico says the new media deal pushes the NBA closer to the NFL's economic model.

Sportico's latest estimates put NBA teams' combined revenue at $13.7 billion, above MLB clubs at $13.2 billion. The baseball figures cover the 2025 calendar season and the basketball figures cover 2025-26, which is the closest like-for-like comparison available.

For sponsorship and partnership teams, the share tells you more than the total. With 41% coming from central revenue, the remaining 59% (our arithmetic) is the local business the club sells itself: tickets, suites, sponsorships, concessions, merchandise, local media and arena events. A brand buying a team partnership deals with that local side. And that side explains the gap between the league's top and bottom clubs.

Team revenue ranged from $895 million for the Golden State Warriors to $339 million for the Memphis Grizzlies. Both figures are after revenue sharing, which moved roughly $400 million to lower-revenue teams. High-revenue clubs and 50% of luxury tax proceeds fund that pool.

Sportico's $13.7 billion team figure is net of revenue sharing and includes non-NBA events, such as concerts, at buildings teams own or operate. The $14.5 billion league figure is larger because part of it stays with the league for investments and expenses.

Golden State is a different case. The Warriors' revenue rose from $833 million in 2024-25 to $895 million in 2025-26, the most in the league in both seasons. Brady Klopfer of Golden State of Mind points to Chase Center, the privately funded arena the ownership group built in 2019. By building it, he writes, the Warriors have become the landlords to the biggest concerts in the Bay Area, with Doja Cat, Phoebe Bridgers, the Jonas Brothers and Journey booked in the coming weeks. It is also home to the WNBA's Golden State Valkyries, a separate entity under the same ownership that Sportico values at $850 million.

Golden State led the league with $895 million in team revenue in 2025-26, according to Sportico. When a club controls its building and keeps it busy on non-game nights, local revenue can grow faster than the league's shared money.

Memphis shows the other side. The Grizzlies had the lowest revenue in Sportico's figures in both seasons, at $301 million in 2024-25 and $339 million in 2025-26. Those totals are net of revenue sharing. High-revenue teams and 50% of luxury tax proceeds paid for that system, which sent roughly $400 million to low-revenue teams. The same per-team national TV payout is a much larger share of a $339 million budget than of an $895 million one.

Local media was a weak point in 2024-25. Sportico reported that basketball-related income came to $10.25 billion that season. That figure, which determines the salary cap, was held down by a choppy local media market and by several small-market teams advancing to the conference finals, which reduced postseason gate receipts. Because of that, teams received more than $480 million from the escrow fund, which exists to keep revenue divided 51-49 between players and owners. Partners with deals tied to regional broadcast inventory should keep a close eye on the local media numbers.

The league has global ambitions, including plans to build new leagues in Africa and Europe, and it has a new blockbuster TV contract. Together, those have led investors to push up the price of owning 1/30th of it. Sportico puts the average franchise at $6.64 billion, up 21% in a year and 157% from $2.58 billion in 2021. Memphis, the lowest-valued club, is worth $4.2 billion, 2.8 times its 2021 value of $1.51 billion.

According to signals from the league, a call on expansion franchises in Las Vegas and Seattle should come before the year ends. One detail is worth tracking: Sportico's $281 million per-team TV projection assumes a 30-team league. If the league grows to 32 teams, that assumption no longer holds.

title: Bemidji State hops into NCAA's new advertising game, with more likely on the way
article_text:
BEMIDJI — On Jan. 23, the NCAA approved the use of sponsorship patches on uniforms in Division I sports for the first time.

Many universities took advantage early — Wisconsin reached a deal with Culver’s, Ohio State with JPMorgan Chase. Even the entire Big 12 conference reached a sponsorship/naming rights deal with Monster Energy.

But the new ruling applied to Division I sports only. That meant only the men's and women's hockey teams at Bemidji State had new real estate for sale.

As Bemidji State’s assistant director of athletics for development and sponsorship, Katz is in charge of recruiting companies for ads seen at places like the Sanford Center and Chet Anderson Stadium. After the ruling in January, he was tasked with finding a company to partner with that would benefit the hockey programs financially, but would also be a good fit.

It was also key for Katz and the school to avoid rushing into a partnership, a strategy that most D-I programs across the country have taken. Bigger schools like the University of Minnesota and North Dakota, for example, have yet to stitch ad patches.

“We had our mind set on it pretty early,” Katz said. “It was something that we wanted to advertise and get out there. And we still have opportunities available for a business to come in and put a logo on our jersey, and that’s something that we’re going to continue to explore, even as the season progresses.

“So I think we wanted to proceed quickly, but also with some caution.”

As soon as both hockey teams hit the ice in October, they donned their new jersey sponsor: Paul Bunyan Communications, featured on the left side of the chest on all jerseys.

Two more sponsorship opportunities are still available. Bemidji State can add one more patch on its jerseys and can have a helmet sponsor.

But finding new ad revenue hasn’t stopped at uniform sponsors. After the NCAA allowed ads on football fields in 2024, that paved the way for Bemidji State to partner with local companies to help fund the new turf at Chet Anderson Stadium.

Soon, Bemidji State expects the NCAA to allow jersey ads for D-II sports, opening the gates for more sponsorship deals for other sports on campus.

With changes come detractors. Traditionalists frown upon sponsorship patches, seeing their school's uniform as sacred. But even Notre Dame, perhaps the most traditional school in the country, now features a sponsor (Sofi Technologies) on its iconic football jerseys.

In a new era of college sports, schools are constantly seeking more revenue. That’s been taxing for some programs after the 2025 House settlement, which opened the doors for schools to pay their athletes money from Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) directly.

While BSU opted out of the House settlement, both its men’s and women’s hockey teams play against schools that have greater resources and more NIL opportunities for their players. Revenue from the jersey sponsorships goes directly to the programs.

“You find a sponsor patch for the women’s hockey program, and that funding is going towards the women’s hockey program," Katz said. "So it’s extremely important, whether that’s paying for pucks for the year, or tape, skates, helmets — whatever you need.”

Bemidji State has already seen how sponsors can help improve a particular aspect of a program. They’ve seen that happen just this year, when BSU replaced its aging turf at Chet Anderson Stadium with a new National Football League-approved turf, one of the first of its kind in D-II.

The funding for the field was achieved with the help of sponsors. Unlike on-ice advertisers at the Sanford Center, which can be easily replaced once their contracts are up, turf logos are permanent.

Helping BSU fund the project was appealing to many in the local businesses. First National Bank and Federated Insurance pitched in to help fund the new turf. Both companies now have their logos featured at every event at Chet Anderson Stadium, from BSU football, women's soccer and softball to Bemidji High School athletics.

“They were pretty quick turnarounds,” Katz said. “Utilizing corporate sponsors helped secure partial funding of the turf. We had some other donors that helped support it as well, but that’s ultimately where those sponsorship opportunities became a thing.”

The prospect of being featured on Bemidji State’s hockey jerseys also became appealing to Bemidji businesses. But finding a sponsor isn’t as simple as putting up a picture of a jersey on Facebook Marketplace saying “Place your ad here.”

Instead, it’s a combination of Katz reaching out to those in the Bemidji business community, and businesses reaching out to him.

“We are definitely aggressive when it comes to outreach,” he said. “There is a little bit of word of mouth, or wanting to reach out to us to learn a little bit more. I mean, I get emails and calls frequently from somebody who saw an advertisement at a hockey game or a football game and wanted to know how they could have an advertisement of their own.”

In the end, Paul Bunyan Communications, a longtime partner with Bemidji State hockey, became the first jersey sponsor in BSU history. Katz is still kicking tires on other deals as well, which could be added during the season.

title: Classic Sportswear and NRL Extend Representative Apparel Partnership
article_text:
Australian sportswear manufacturer Classic Sportswear has officially executed a multi-year partnership extension with the National Rugby League (NRL) and the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC).

Announced ahead of the Rugby League World Cup Finals at Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium, the agreement ensures Classic remains the official on-field and retail apparel partner for the Australian Kangaroos, Australian Jillaroos, Indigenous All Stars, Māori All Stars, and NRL Match Officials.

Tracing its rugby league heritage back to 1934, Classic Sportswear continues a long-standing commercial alignment that encompasses major international campaigns and retail fan-engagement programmes.

Beyond outfitting elite national and representative squads, the extended contract cements Classic’s ongoing backing of the NRL’s consumer-focused $99 jersey pricing initiative, designed to maintain retail affordability across supporter merchandise.

Classic Sportswear CEO, Ross Smart, highlighted the brand’s nine-decade heritage within rugby league and its ongoing commitment to representative pathways.

“Classic Sportswear’s commitment to Australia’s national Rugby League teams runs deep and carries through to this Rugby League World Cup, where we are thrilled to announce the continuation of our partnership with the Kangaroos, Jillaroos and the Australian Rugby League Commission.”

“Classic has proudly been there for so many great Australian moments – from the unbeaten 1986 Kangaroo Tour and World Cup triumphs in 1988 and 2000 to, more recently, Pacific Championships victories by both the Kangaroos and Jillaroos.

“Having been part of the fabric of Rugby League since 1934, we are genuine partners to the game, its clubs, players and officials.

“We look forward to carrying that proud tradition into the new term across the Kangaroos, Jillaroos, All Stars teams and Match Officials, while continuing to innovate and create for the next generation of players and fans,” Smart said.

ARLC executive chairman, Peter V’landys AM, emphasised the commercial importance of Classic’s support for affordable supporter apparel.

“Classic have been loyal partners of Rugby League for many years and I’m sure they will continue to be part of the game for many more.”

“Classic have been strong supporters of the NRL’s $99 jersey initiative. It is important for the NRL and Classic that jerseys are affordable especially in a cost of living crisis,” V’landys said.

title: Shaw and Partners Financial Services Extends Manly Warringah Sea Eagles Partnership Through 2029
article_text:
Investment and wealth management firm Shaw and Partners Financial Services has executed a three-year commercial partnership extension with National Rugby League (NRL) club the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles.

The renewed agreement takes effect from the 2027 NRL season and runs through to the end of 2029, extending an unbroken commercial alliance that first commenced in 2018.

Under the extended contract, Shaw and Partners retains prominent sleeve branding placement across both the Sea Eagles’ flagship NRL playing kit and all junior Pathways jerseys.

The multi-year renewal secures consistent commercial backing across every tier of Manly’s football operations, reinforcing corporate stability as the club prepares for its 2027 campaign at 4 Pines Park.

Shaw and Partners Financial Services CEO, Earl Evans, highlighted the firm’s long-standing commitment to the club’s heritage and talent pathways.

“We’re incredibly proud of our association with the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles and what we’ve built together since 2018.”

“Over that time, the relationship has continued to grow, and we’re pleased to reaffirm our commitment to the Club for the next three seasons.

“Manly is a club with a proud history, a passionate supporter base and a strong commitment to developing the next generation of talent.

“We are looking forward to continuing our support across both the NRL and Pathways programs,” Evans said.

Manly Warringah Sea Eagles CEO, Jason King, emphasised the importance of securing multi-year corporate support across the club’s entire football structure.

“Shaw and Partners has been an outstanding supporter of the Sea Eagles since 2018, and their continued investment is a strong endorsement of the direction we’re heading as a Club.”

“Having partners who believe in what we’re building and commit to supporting not just our NRL team, but our entire football program is incredibly important.

“We’re extremely grateful for Earl and the team’s ongoing support and look forward to building on the partnership over the coming seasons,” King said.

title: Qatar to raise hosting standards even higher as football fever begins: Hassan Al Kuwari
article_text:
Qatar is all set once again for football fever with the on-going international friendlies, the about to begin FIFA U17 World Cup Qatar 2026, the forthcoming FIFA Intercontinental Cup, the Qatar-UAE Super Cup, and the Qatar Cup final.

“Qatar is now the sports capital of the world, especially when it comes to football. Everyone would like Qatar to host a tournament or a match like a final,” said Hassan bin Rabiah Al Kuwari, the Local Organizing Committee (LOC) Executive Director of Marketing, Promotions, Events and Commercial Affairs during a Media Roundtable at the Al Bidda Tower on Sunday.

“We are set to organize numerous tournaments and matches in the coming period, and Qatar is fully ready to welcome teams and national squads. So far, 30 national teams have arrived for FIFA U17 World Cup Qatar 2026 and the tournament will be held as scheduled, and we expect it to be a great success,” he added.

Speaking about the packed calendar and back-to-back big tournaments and the readiness for it, Al Kuwari said, “We are working with all our stakeholders to deliver the best experience for everyone.

“It’s also a part of tourism aspect, which is very important for Qatar. We are quite fine. And Inshallah, we will try to get more and more (events).”

The FIFA U17 World Cup is the second successive edition being held in Qatar, featuring 48 teams and 104 matches. There will also be a wide range of accompanying events, as the tournament has evolved into a comprehensive sports and entertainment festival for everyone taking place at the Aspire Zone.

The tournament begins on November 19, with the final on December 13.

“We are also aiming to showcase the diversity of our facilities. While the final was held at Khalifa International Stadium last year, this year it will be hosted at Ahmad Bin Ali Stadium.”

With regard to the FIFA Intercontinental Cup, Al Kuwari said, “We have several important competitions lined up, building on the success of previous editions. Matches are scheduled for December 9, 12, and 16, with the final set to be held at Ahmad Bin Ali Stadium. The tournament, which will feature teams like Paris Saint-Germain, is highly significant for football fans. It encompasses three distinct competitions: the Challenge Cup, the Elite Cup, and the aforementioned tournament. We wish everyone the best of luck, and we look forward to welcoming teams from across the globe.

“Additionally, there is another tournament (Qatar Cup final between Al Sadd and Al Rayyan) which I expect will also generate great excitement. The final at the Khalifa International Stadium between two teams that command a large fan base. It has been quite some time since these teams met at this level.”

The Qatar Super Cup will take place from December 17th to 20th, featuring four matches: two held in Qatar and two in the United Arab Emirates.

“We have endeavoured to centralize these events within Qatar to enhance the fan experience, and tickets will be available for purchase digitally.

“Additionally, there will be several international matches, including Qatar versus Australia, Qatar versus South Korea, Saudi Arabia versus South Korea, and Saudi Arabia versus Pakistan,” he informed.

He stressed: “Qatar is fully prepared, with its infrastructure and facilities ready. The venues are set to host spectators, who will be able to attend various matches and enjoy the accompanying events. We have carefully managed the entry and exit processes for the diverse crowds.Based on figures from previous editions, we anticipate an average of 10,000 spectators per match. We also look forward to welcoming a wide variety of fans from different nations.

“Furthermore, we are collaborating with various partners, including those on digital platforms like YouTube, to facilitate direct access, such as through official links provided by the respective federations. Should any federation have specific requests, we are fully prepared to accommodate them, for instance, for teams from countries like Algeria or Saudi Arabia, to ensure everything is well-organized.

“There is a strong commitment to maintaining clear communication with the various Arab communities. We actively engage with them to facilitate their attendance and provide detailed information, especially since the tournament is being held in an Arab nation.

“We are in constant contact with the leadership of these fan groups, such as those representing communities from Morocco or Saudi Arabia, to offer them support. In previous tournaments, we witnessed great enthusiasm in the stands. The various fan groups truly enriched the competition.

“This ongoing dialogue extends beyond just this tournament. We consistently stay in touch with the leaders of these fan groups and the expatriate communities residing in the host country. I believe Qatar will continue to demonstrate its capabilities.

“As an organizing committee, we are constantly striving to surpass the benchmarks we have already set and to raise our standards even higher.

“Hosting a large number of tournaments and matches simultaneously is something we are well-accustomed to. Thank God, we possess the necessary expertise, human resources, world-class facilities, and infrastructure, both within and beyond the realm of sports, to manage such a scale.

“We have successfully hosted numerous major events, including the FIFA World Cup, MotoGP, Arab Cup, Intercontinental Cup, and various youth tournaments, often concurrently, all executed to an exceptionally high standard.

“With every event, we aim to reach new heights and enhance the overall experience, for the fans, the participating teams, and the media alike. We are committed to continuously improving and delivering an even better experience each time.”

title: Sunshine Stars partner firm for sponsorship deal
article_text:
The Sunshine Stars Football Club of Akure , Ondo State has partnered a firm – The Sunbeth Nigeria Limited in the area of sponsorship of the club.

The Ondo State darling club said the development was meant to improve the performance of the club in the ongoing Nigeria National League.

The President of Sunshine Stars Football Club, Mr Divine Ogbonaya, who spoke on the development on Sunday, said the sponsorship deal was facilitated by another firm , The Solution Check, describing it as a dream come true and a morale booster for the team.

He said, “ This agreement will go a long way in motivating the players and club officials. We are using this opportunity to appeal to the sponsor to extend the partnership to other teams under the management of the agency.

“We still have female teams, Sunshine Queens, Sunshine U19, Sunshine U17 and U15.”

He attributed the club’s recent progress to the foundation laid by the ODSFA board less than a year ago, adding that two players developed under its watch had represented Nigeria at the FIFA U20 World Cup.

“The foundation we laid less than a year ago is beginning to yield results. Within a short period in office, we have been able to produce two players who have represented Nigeria at the U20 World Cup.

“If you visit the Game Village in Oda, you will ask: ‘Are you sure this is Ondo State?’ We are laying a very solid foundation in line with the directive of our Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa. There are still better things to come, and we will continue to work hard.”

“We will continue to motivate the players and officials by paying their winning bonuses and salaries regularly,” he added.

In his remarks, Sunbeth’s Head of Warehouse Operations and Compliance, Adebayo Kupoluyi, said the organisation was interested in partnering with Sunshine Stars as part of its commitment to investing in local businesses and communities.

He explained that the partnership was driven by the company’s desire to create value for the people, noting that football was an effective platform for connecting communities.

“Our core objective is to create value for our people. We chose football because we believe it connects every member of the community,” Kupoluyi said.

“Football is fun, but at the same time, it is an investment for both the investor and the community.”

In his welcome address, the facilitator and representative of Solution Check, Adedeji Adegbenro, congratulated Sunshine Stars and Sunbeth on what he described as a milestone sponsorship agreement, expressing confidence that both parties would derive value from the partnership.

Adegbenro also highlighted the important role of the media in the partnership, urging journalists to report professionally and objectively while giving attention to positive developments.

“While the media are expected to do their jobs professionally by reporting facts, we urge them to also see the positive side of what we are doing. We appeal to our hardworking journalists to promote Sunshine Stars positively as they begin their 2026/27 NNL campaign.”

He acknowledged that the club’s current position was below its traditional status, but expressed confidence that collective support would help it return to the top flight.

“This is not where Sunshine Stars are supposed to be playing, but with the support of all and sundry, Sunshine Stars FC will return to the elite league, where they truly belong,” he declared.

title: KPMG makes its tech play as Indian sports bloom
article_text:
Bengaluru: India’s sports industry is emerging as a significant business opportunity, with the market projected to reach $42 billion by 2030-31. Growing investments in professional leagues, sports infrastructure, athlete development and digital platforms are opening up opportunities beyond cricket. The 2030 Commonwealth Games and India’s ambition to host the 2036 Olympics could further accelerate spending across the sector.

KPMG in India is positioning itself to tap this opportunity by combining its consulting expertise with technology solutions. The firm has identified 16 sub-sectors across the sports ecosystem and recently unveiled its Sports Technology Hub in Bengaluru, bringing together capabilities in AI, advanced analytics, computer vision- training and match insights and digital platforms.

“The sports industry was around $19 billion in 2025, and this year it is about $21 billion, growing at around 12-14%,” Prasanth Shanthakumaran, Partner and Head of Sports Sector, KPMG in India, tells DH. The firm expects the sector to reach around $42 billion by 2030-31.

A KPMG report, strengthening India’s sports ecosystem, describes the shift from a cricket-dominated entertainment sector to a structured, investable economy. Cricket contributes nearly 85% of the sports economy, but leagues in kabaddi, football, hockey, chess, kho-kho, volleyball, badminton and women’s sports point to the potential of other sporting products.

The Indian Premier League (IPL), with an enterprise value of $20.6 billion, has demonstrated sports’ ability to attract sponsors, broadcasters, investors and consumers.

KPMG’s 16 sub-sectors span governments, federations, clubs, sports education, manufacturing, tourism, the athlete economy, venture capital and sports-focused global capability centres (GCCs), among others. “We are looking at the entire ecosystem of sports. There is going to be massive investment in sports across all areas over the next 10 years. Cricket will dominate, but other sports will also grow,” Shanthakumaran says.

The firm’s sports practice advises clients on business plans, governance, market opportunities, operational strategies and funding. The technology hub complements this work by developing solutions for challenges across the sector.

One priority is grassroots talent identification. Physical tests assessing muscle strength and performance in running and jumping can help identify suitable sports for individuals. Wearables and analytics can monitor athlete performance, flag injury risks and inform training and nutrition.

Infrastructure utilisation is another focus. Despite investments in stadiums and sporting facilities, many remain underused. Digital platforms can connect users with available facilities, while technology can support fan engagement, sponsorship and event management.

Around 80% of KPMG’s sports technology development is expected to be driven by client requirements, with the firm independently investing in solutions where it sees wider market potential.

One initiative is a platform to manage large sporting events, covering transport, event infrastructure, technology implementation and scoreboard management, as well as post-event visitor data. Developed for cities planning large-scale events, it could be offered through a purchase or transaction-based arrangement.

KPMG has also developed an app for an Indian football club, bringing its fan base onto a common platform and creating opportunities for merchandise sales and other revenue streams. Shanthakumaran says such platforms could also enable fans to contribute financially, helping clubs attract funding beyond traditional corporate investment.

The hub showcases applications including AI-powered fan engagement, smart stadium management, athlete analytics, computer vision-based training and match insights, digital ticketing, loyalty solutions and sponsorship measurement. It also covers predictive maintenance, cybersecurity, sustainability and generative AI-enabled content creation.

“Realising India’s potential in sports calls for innovation across the entire sports value-chain. The KPMG Sports Technology Hub aims to bring industry expertise and technology together to help reshape how a sport is played, managed and experienced,” says Yezdi Nagporewalla, CEO, KPMG in India.

The hub is the first such facility established by KPMG globally, and is expected to support international clients. Designed as a collaborative platform, it brings together teams from different functions and clients.

While it has physical components, much of its work is cloud-based, allowing teams across locations to demonstrate and develop solutions. KPMG’s sports technology practice has more than 200 consultants.

Meanwhile, there is scope for varied sports to grow commercially beyond cricket. Sustainable leagues, however, need stronger media rights and sponsorship revenues, the two major sources of commercial income.

Shanthakumaran also points to greater private-sector participation through corporate investment and CSR funding, alongside better utilisation of existing infrastructure. KPMG is working to map sponsorship opportunities for clubs and identify potential revenue streams.
